title: Collaboration in Hybrid Environments: Co-Defining Collaborative Spatial Layouts
researchFocus: Designing interaction techniques that enable geographically distributed collaborators to jointly organize spatial layouts of shared content across heterogeneous display environments (AR, VR, tabletops, and large screens).
collaboration: Remote participants collaboratively arrange and coordinate shared information and spatial workspaces despite differences in their physical environments and display devices.
evaluation: User interviews, prototype development, and controlled user studies are planned. Specific collaboration-quality measures are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Moderately relevant to our proposed research. Shared spatial layouts across AR, VR and other displays may inform cross-device awareness, but this thesis concerns organizing collaborative content rather than group movement or conversational transitions.

title: Real-Time Collaboration in Hybrid Spaces Combining Virtual Environments and Tangible Interfaces
researchFocus: Designing tangible interaction techniques and context-sharing methods to support real-time remote collaboration between AR and VR users under unreliable communication conditions.
collaboration: A remote VR expert collaborates with a local AR operator to perform complex medical or technical procedures through shared contextual information and remote guidance.
evaluation: The proposal examines context sharing and tangible interaction during remote AR–VR expert assistance, with attention to situational understanding, communication constraints and cognitive workload. Detailed team-level collaboration measures are not specified.
myResearch: Moderate connection through asymmetric AR–VR collaboration and shared situational awareness. Its emphasis on tangible interfaces, remote expert assistance and communication disruptions differs from our investigation of moving groups and changing conversations at hybrid events.

title: Editing and Synchronizing Digital Twins in VR and AR for the Factory of the Future
researchFocus: Developing collaborative AR–VR interaction techniques to jointly edit industrial digital twins while synchronizing changes between physical and virtual environments.
collaboration: On-site AR operators and remote VR engineers jointly modify and update a shared 3D digital twin of a factory.
example: A factory technician wearing AR glasses and a remote VR engineer collaboratively reposition machinery in a digital factory model and synchronize their changes.
evaluation: Planned evaluations of collaborative VR editing and asymmetric AR–VR collaboration. Specific team-level collaboration measures are not defined.
myResearch: Moderately relevant: coordinating on-site AR operators and remote VR collaborators offers transferable approaches to shared spatial understanding, although the research centers on editing industrial digital twins rather than informal group interaction.

title: THandgibles: A Hand-Centered Approach to Collaborative Tangible Interaction
researchFocus: Developing hand-tracking techniques to recognize and manipulate ordinary physical objects as tangible interfaces without markers or sensors attached to them.
collaboration: Multiple AR users manipulate and exchange physical objects to share digital information, transfer roles, and maintain awareness of each other's actions.
example: Two designers wearing AR headsets exchange a physical object to transfer associated digital information during a shared design task.
evaluation: Investigating the reliability and limitations of hand-based object manipulation recognition. Specific collaboration-quality evaluation methods are not described.
myResearch: Low relevance to our proposal. Hand-tracked tangible object exchange offers some insight into collaborative awareness, but this research addresses object manipulation rather than remote participation or dynamic group transitions.

title: Designing Tools for Collaboration During Practical Work in Virtual Reality
researchFocus: Designing VR interaction techniques to support collaborative practical learning, particularly in neuroscience education.
collaboration: Remote students collaborate in shared VR environments through communication, action coordination, awareness of others' activities, and joint manipulation of virtual objects.
evaluation: Requirements gathering with students and teachers, development of an interactive VR environment, and user evaluation are planned. Specific collaboration-quality measures are not defined.
myResearch: Moderate relevance through collaborative awareness, communication and coordination among people sharing a VR space. The project studies practical learning tasks rather than movement and social participation across co-located AR and remote VR groups.

title: Collaborative Immersive Artistic Performances
researchFocus: Designing immersive interaction techniques that enable artists and audiences to collaboratively create and influence artistic performances in VR/MR.
collaboration: Artists and audiences jointly shape an immersive performance through asymmetric interaction, with artists having greater control than spectators.
example: Musicians collaboratively manipulate a virtual musical instrument while VR spectators influence visual effects during the performance.
evaluation: Planned laboratory and artistic-performance evaluations of interaction, co-presence, expressiveness, audience understanding and perceived agency; proposed measures are not yet validated project findings.
myResearch: Moderate connection to our proposed research, particularly in asymmetric participation, social interaction and coordination among participants with different roles. However, it focuses on collaborative artistic performances rather than spatial and social transitions between remote VR and co-located AR participants.

title: PhyDiViews: Collaboration in Hybrid Environments (AR, VR, Desktop): Multi-Views with Different Physicalities and Dimensions
researchFocus: Designing techniques to share, synchronize, and transition between different 2D/3D viewpoints across heterogeneous AR, VR, and desktop environments.
collaboration: Remote experts and on-site AR users coordinate 2D/3D viewpoints, share annotations, and may use physical movement guidance to align relevant perspectives on physical or virtual objects.
example: A remote VR expert examines a virtual machine from different angles and guides an on-site AR technician to the correct physical viewpoint to inspect a faulty component.
evaluation: The proposal describes controlled studies of collaborative viewpoint techniques, including task performance, spatial awareness, workload and co-presence; these are planned evaluation directions.
myResearch: Moderate connection through coordinated AR–VR viewpoints, physical navigation guidance and spatial awareness. These approaches could inform hybrid group movement, although the project primarily investigates viewpoint coordination for remote assistance rather than conversational and group-membership transitions.

title: Shared Immersive Environments for Artistic Co-Creation with Heterogeneous Modalities
researchFocus: Designing shared immersive XR environments that enable artists to collaboratively create using different artistic modalities (music, dance, 3D drawing).
collaboration: Remote artists jointly create digital artworks by connecting their different interaction modalities.
example: A dancer's movements control a musician's sound effects, while the music dynamically changes a 3D artist's virtual drawing tools.
evaluation: The proposal anticipates controlled studies of how heterogeneous creative modalities support joint understanding and interaction, potentially followed by longer-term work with artists.
myResearch: Only indirectly related to our research: coordinating artists using different creative modalities illustrates collaboration across interfaces, but does not investigate mixed-presence group movement or spontaneous conversational entry.

title: Social Haptics: Study of Haptic Feedback for Promoting Positive Social Interactions in Virtual Reality
researchFocus: Designing and evaluating haptic feedback techniques, particularly speech-synchronized vibrations, to promote positive social interactions in shared VR environments.
collaboration: Investigating how haptic cues accompanying verbal communication influence social presence, persuasion, and leadership among participants in shared VR environments.
evaluation: Proposed evaluation of speech-synchronized vibrations and their influence on social presence and interpersonal communication; team-level collaboration measures are not specified in detail.
myResearch: Low relevance to our proposal. Speech-linked haptic cues may inform nonverbal feedback and social presence, while persuasive tactile communication falls outside our spatial and social transition questions.

title: Learning Through Kinaesthetic Collaboration and Brain Synchrony
researchFocus: Investigating how kinaesthetic (movement and force-based) feedback supports collaborative gesture learning and how it relates to brain synchronization.
collaboration: Two participants coordinate movements through physical guidance to learn motor skills, such as piano playing or dancing, with potential applications to human–robot cooperation.
evaluation: EEG measurements of inter-brain synchronization during collaborative learning, comparing passive and active kinaesthetic feedback.
myResearch: Low relevance. Guided movement and brain synchrony may contribute to broader PC1 evaluation discussions, but the central work investigates kinesthetic skill learning rather than hybrid-group coordination.

title: InstaBeam: Instant Beaming into Immersive Viewing Environments
researchFocus: Exploring rapid capture and sharing of real physical surroundings with remote immersive viewers, including the technical challenges of presenting physical environments across different immersive setups.
collaboration: Investigates how people at a real site and remote immersive viewers can share a representation of the physical setting; specific multi-person collaboration tasks are not the primary focus.
evaluation: The proposal emphasizes technical feasibility and remote immersive viewing. Detailed team-level collaboration outcomes are not specified.
myResearch: Moderate relevance as a possible enabling approach for bringing real-world surroundings into remote immersive views. The project addresses environment capture and representation, not the coordination of walking participants or conversational group membership.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Joint Actions in Collaborative Digital Environments: Co-gestures and Sense of Agency
researchFocus: Investigating collaborative gestures and sense of agency during joint actions in multi-user digital environments.
collaboration: Two users coordinate gestures to jointly manipulate digital objects (moving, zooming, merging, or passing objects).
evaluation: Planned behavioral experiments of coordinated gesture actions and the sense of agency during joint object manipulation.
myResearch: Low relevance through joint-action timing, gesture interpretation and shared agency. The thesis studies dyadic object manipulation rather than multi-person spatial and social transitions.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: CoPilot: Analysis and Design of Interactions and Collaborations to Support Pedestrian Mobility
researchFocus: Designing accessible interaction techniques to support pedestrian navigation through remote caregiver assistance.
collaboration: A person with an intellectual disability and a remote caregiver coordinate to navigate safely to a destination.
evaluation: User-centered evaluations using simulated pedestrian mobility scenarios to assess interaction and collaboration. Specific collaboration-quality metrics are not defined.
myResearch: An indirect connection through remote assistance during physical walking and accessibility; CoPilot addresses pedestrian support rather than coordinated AR–VR group movement.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Remote Collaboration Strategies for Everyday Public Spaces
researchFocus: Designing socially acceptable XR interaction techniques and adaptive virtual layouts for remote collaboration in public spaces.
collaboration: Remote XR users collaborate while adapting their gestures, communication, and virtual layouts to public environments.
evaluation: Planned prototype and laboratory evaluations of socially acceptable XR interaction, participant placement, performance and collaboration in public settings.
myResearch: Moderately relevant, especially to our social-transition challenge: socially acceptable gestures, remote placement and awareness of public surroundings could inform spontaneous group encounters, though this project examines remote collaboration in separate public spaces.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Keeping Collaboration Along Transitions Between Places in VR
researchFocus: Designing interaction techniques that maintain group cohesion, social presence, and collaborative awareness when moving between places in social VR.
collaboration: Multiple VR users coordinate navigation and transitions between virtual locations while maintaining group awareness and ongoing collaboration. Example: A group attending a virtual conference moves together from a presentation room to another venue without losing members or interrupting their shared activity.
evaluation: The proposal outlines field/ethnographic investigations and controlled studies of group movement, cohesion, presence and collaboration continuity during transitions; these are proposed studies, not verified results.
myResearch: Strong connection to our spatial-transition challenge. Both projects investigate how people move together while preserving group cohesion, mutual awareness and collaborative continuity; our study extends the question from all-VR groups to physically walking AR and remote VR participants.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: AVATOUCH: Synchronous Cooperation Based on Social Intention for Virtual Object Manipulation
crossPcNote: Listed under PC1 CATS; explicitly funded by PC5 (cross-PC thesis).
researchFocus: Investigating how intentional gestures and social touch (haptic feedback) improve cooperation between remote users represented by avatars in immersive VR environments.
collaboration: Two remote users in connected immersive rooms cooperate to manipulate virtual objects without verbal communication, relying on gestures and haptic cues. Example: Person A moves a virtual glass toward Person B, who recognizes the intention and fills it using a virtual bottle.
evaluation: Proposed studies of movement intention, gesture and haptic feedback during cooperative object manipulation, including coordination and shared task success.
myResearch: Low relevance to our proposal. Nonverbal intentions and haptic feedback during object cooperation offer a limited conceptual link but do not address group navigation or entry into social conversations.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Exploring the Potential of the Industrial Metaverse in Systems Architecting
researchFocus: Designing adaptive 3D interfaces and shared virtual environments to support collaborative design of complex engineering systems.
collaboration: Engineering experts from different disciplines jointly design and review complex systems using heterogeneous devices (VR, CAVE, desktop, interactive walls). Example: Mechanical and manufacturing engineers collaboratively review an aircraft landing-gear design, using different visual representations to identify and resolve design issues.
evaluation: The proposal considers controlled evaluations and application studies of engineering collaboration across immersive displays; completed outcome measures should not be inferred from the proposal.
myResearch: Only broadly connected. Heterogeneous immersive displays and collaborative engineering workflows raise some common infrastructure concerns, but the central objective is complex systems design rather than dynamic group interaction.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Towards Improving Collective Intelligence in Virtual Reality
researchFocus: Investigating collective intelligence and group dynamics in immersive VR environments. The project examines verbal and nonverbal communication cues to develop interaction techniques that improve group collaboration and collective learning.
collaboration: Multiple participants collaborate on shared tasks in immersive VR environments. The project investigates how communication patterns, group behavior, and collective intelligence influence teamwork and collaborative learning.
evaluation: The project proposes investigating relationships between collective intelligence, verbal and nonverbal cues, and group dynamics in VR. Specific experimental protocols and collaboration-quality measures are not described in the available abstract.
myResearch: Moderate conceptual relevance through VR group dynamics and verbal/nonverbal communication patterns, which may help frame collaboration measures. It does not directly study hybrid AR–VR navigation or changes in group membership.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Study of Interpersonal Haptic Interactions Between Virtual Avatars
researchFocus: Designing and evaluating interpersonal haptic interaction techniques that simulate realistic physical contact between virtual avatars. The project investigates how multisensory feedback influences immersion, emotional responses, and interpersonal interactions in collaborative VR training environments.
collaboration: Trainees and instructors interact within shared VR training environments using avatars and haptic devices. The project explores synchronized multisensory interactions that support collaborative training, interpersonal communication, and responses to stressful situations.
evaluation: Planned investigations of how haptic feedback affects user experience and emotional responses during virtual interactions. Measures include perceived stress, presence, co-presence, physiological signals, and behavioral responses. Specific measures of collaborative task performance are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Low relevance: interpersonal touch and avatar embodiment provide background for social cues, while this project concerns haptic physical contact in VR training rather than hybrid-event conversations.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: MuseoXR: Archaeological Exhibits in Museography with Collaborative Extended Reality
researchFocus: Designing collaborative XR environments that enable museum professionals and public audiences to co-create archaeological exhibitions. The project investigates immersive interaction techniques for combining physical artefacts, virtual content, and remote archaeological environments.
collaboration: Museum curators, scenographers, and public visitors collaboratively design and develop archaeological exhibitions using VR and AR technologies. The project explores participatory co-creation, enabling visitors to contribute feedback and creative input during the exhibition design process.
evaluation: Planned user research with museum professionals, participatory co-design, and prototype development. The project proposes evaluating collaborative exhibition-design workflows. Specific experimental measures of collaboration quality are not defined.
myResearch: An indirect relationship to our work. Collaborative XR exhibition design is a potential application context, but its principal questions involve museum co-creation rather than informal movement and social transitions.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Enabling Subtle Visual Modifications with AR+AI
researchFocus: Developing real-time AI techniques that enable subtle visual modifications of physical environments and social cues through AR headsets. The project investigates generative AI, distributed computing, and real-time image, video, and 3D rendering.
collaboration: The proposed application concerns face-to-face social interactions where AR users perceive AI-modified environmental elements and conversational cues. However, the thesis primarily investigates the technical infrastructure for real-time visual modification rather than specific collaborative tasks or group coordination.
evaluation: Planned technical evaluations of image-generation speed, visual quality, temporal consistency, and real-time rendering performance. The project aims to improve generation from 20 to 60 FPS and extend techniques to 3D and video. Specific evaluations of collaborative effectiveness are not described.
myResearch: Low relevance. AI-mediated visual cues may eventually influence how participants perceive one another, but the thesis prioritizes real-time rendering rather than coordination of evolving groups.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Detecting (Inter)actions of a Remote AR Operator Collaborating with a VR Expert for Assistance in Isolated Environments
researchFocus: Developing AI-based techniques to recognize physical actions performed by remote AR users using multimodal data and activity models. The project investigates how action recognition can improve situational awareness and adaptive remote assistance in isolated environments.
collaboration: A remote AR operator and a VR expert collaborate on critical medical or technical tasks across geographically isolated environments. The system communicates the operator's actions and task progress to the expert, enabling informed decisions and adaptive guidance despite communication delays or interruptions.
evaluation: The proposal aims to validate the techniques in realistic space-medicine scenarios with potential support from CNES, ESA, and MEDES. Specific experimental protocols and measures of collaborative effectiveness are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Only indirectly related despite the AR–VR asymmetry: recognizing an operator’s actions for expert assistance supports task monitoring, not transitions between walking groups or social conversations.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Materialising Socio-emotional Presence in Collaborative Learning and Work
crossPcNote: Cross-PC PC1/PC5 thesis listed under PC5, explicitly funded by PC1.
researchFocus: Investigating how nonverbal emotional expression affects group collaboration and whether tangible, multisensory feedback can help teams understand and regulate shared socio-emotional presence.
collaboration: Primarily co-located groups of four to eight learners working on collaborative problem-solving tasks, with an emphasis on group emotional awareness, regulation and the acceptability of sharing affective information.
evaluation: Proposed design-based research combining observations, interviews, co-design of tangible feedback, and comparisons of group interaction with and without emotional-presence cues, including ethical and privacy considerations.
myResearch: Moderately relevant to the social experience of collaboration: its measures of nonverbal affect and group emotional regulation could complement our evaluations, although the project studies collaborative learning with tangible feedback rather than hybrid-event transitions.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Investigating Benefits and Limitations of Asymmetric Collaboration for Designing Sensory Experiences in Mixed Reality
researchFocus: Investigating the benefits and limitations of asymmetric collaboration for designing sensory experiences, particularly vibrotactile and pseudo-haptic feedback, in mixed-reality environments. The project examines whether combining immersive VR interaction with precise desktop controls improves collaborative design compared with individual workflows.
collaboration: Two designers collaborate synchronously using heterogeneous VR and desktop environments to jointly develop sensory experiences. The project investigates communication, task allocation, shared control of design parameters, and coordination between collaborators performing parallel or sequential activities.
evaluation: Planned comparisons between asymmetric collaborative design and individual workflows involving switching between VR and desktop environments. The research investigates workflow efficiency, communication challenges, workload distribution, and the benefits of parallel versus sequential collaboration. Specific experimental measures are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Low relevance. Its study of roles, shared control and division of work across VR and desktop settings offers general lessons, but designing sensory experiences differs from supporting dynamic hybrid groups.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Asymmetric Remote Collaboration for Physical Therapy and Implications on Rehabilitation/Movement Guidance
researchFocus: Designing asymmetric AR–VR collaboration techniques that enable remote physiotherapists to guide patients during rehabilitation exercises. The project investigates user representation, interaction modalities, and feedback techniques for effective remote movement guidance.
collaboration: A remote VR therapist and a local AR patient collaborate synchronously to perform rehabilitation exercises. The therapist observes and guides the patient's movements through verbal and nonverbal communication, while both participants coordinate their actions across different immersive environments.
evaluation: Planned prototype development and user studies involving physiotherapists and patients. Evaluations investigate user representation, interaction techniques, and visual and haptic feedback for remote rehabilitation. Specific collaboration-quality measures are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Moderately related through asymmetrical AR–VR participation, movement guidance and user representations. The primary objective, however, is one-to-one rehabilitation assistance rather than socially coordinated group locomotion.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Augmenting Workspace Awareness with Passive BCI: From Monitoring to Enhancing Team Coordination
researchFocus: Investigating whether passive Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) can identify neural markers of collaborative coordination, misalignment, and mutual misunderstanding. The project explores EEG-based neurofeedback to enhance workspace awareness and team coordination.
collaboration: Two or three co-located participants collaborate synchronously on shared tasks, transitioning between loosely and tightly coupled collaboration. The project investigates whether EEG-based measures can detect changes in collaborative coupling and support mutual understanding and coordination.
evaluation: Planned controlled experiments comparing different collaboration conditions using shared and separate displays, including scenarios involving miscommunication. Evaluations examine EEG marker reliability, classification accuracy, and objective and subjective collaboration quality when neurofeedback is introduced.
myResearch: Moderate methodological relevance: transitions between loosely and tightly coupled teamwork and measures of shared awareness could inform our evaluation design. EEG-based feedback in co-located task work is otherwise outside our research scope.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: PARMI: Personalised and Accessible Extended Reality Musical Instruments for Practitioners–Patients Collaboration in Music Therapy
researchFocus: Designing personalized and accessible XR musical instruments that support collaborative music-making between therapists and autistic children. The project investigates adaptive interaction techniques that accommodate different cognitive, sensory, and motor abilities.
collaboration: Therapists and patients collaborate synchronously in shared physical spaces using mixed-reality headsets. The project explores asymmetric collaboration, where participants with different abilities jointly interact with virtual musical instruments during individual or group therapy sessions.
evaluation: Planned interviews, participatory design workshops, controlled usability studies, and long-term evaluations during real music-therapy sessions. Evaluations investigate accessibility, collaborative experience, co-presence, communication, therapeutic benefits, and changes in participant behavior.
myResearch: A limited connection through accessible, personalized mixed-reality collaboration; the project concentrates on therapeutic music-making rather than remote–co-located group transitions.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Collaborative Exploration of Alternative Problem-Solving Approaches Using VR and AR for the Factory of the Future
researchFocus: Designing asymmetric AR–VR collaboration techniques that enable remote experts and on-site operators to explore alternative solutions to complex industrial problems. The project investigates how virtual environments and physical constraints can be combined to support collaborative problem-solving.
collaboration: An on-site AR operator and a remote VR expert collaboratively solve industrial problems across physical and virtual environments. The expert explores possible solutions in VR, while the operator evaluates their feasibility in the physical environment. Both iteratively refine solutions through shared information and coordinated interaction.
evaluation: The proposal discusses evaluating user comfort, fatigue, perceptual biases, cybersickness, and the acceptability of XR devices in realistic industrial settings. Specific experimental methods and measures of collaborative problem-solving effectiveness are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Moderate connection via on-site AR and remote VR participants coordinating around differing physical constraints. This work studies industrial problem-solving, not sustained walk-and-talk or changing conversational groups.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Collective Activities in Immersive Teleclinics for Mental Health Prevention
researchFocus: Designing and evaluating collective and collaborative activities in immersive VR environments for mental health prevention. The project investigates group dynamics, different levels of collaboration, and tools for healthcare professionals to supervise and support group activities.
collaboration: Patients participate in synchronous group activities within shared VR environments, either independently or under healthcare professional supervision. The project investigates how individual activities can become collaborative, how practitioners facilitate group interactions, and how collaboration is maintained across recurring sessions.
evaluation: Planned studies and observation of VR group discussions and collaborative activities with participants and clinicians, including engagement, group dynamics, usability and acceptance.
myResearch: Moderately relevant to group facilitation and social participation in shared VR, especially how participants move between individual and collective activities. Its clinical aims and all-VR setting differ from informal hybrid-event interaction.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Designing Persuasive Haptic Feedback to Support Social Interactions in Mixed Reality
researchFocus: Designing persuasive haptic feedback techniques that enhance verbal communication, social presence, persuasion, and interpersonal interactions in collaborative mixed-reality environments.
collaboration: Small groups of two to four participants collaborate synchronously across heterogeneous VR, AR, and desktop environments. Haptic feedback supports interpersonal communication, collective decision-making, conflict resolution, and group coordination.
evaluation: Planned user experiments investigating different haptic modalities, body locations, and speech-synchronized feedback techniques. Measures include co-presence, subjective haptic experience, physiological responses, and movement data. Specific measures of collective task performance are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Low relevance to our current questions. Although the project investigates social communication in mixed-reality groups, its main contribution is speech-synchronized persuasive haptics rather than spatial coordination or conversational group entry.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Videoconferencing in On-the-Go Contexts: Collaboration Challenges and Interaction Design
researchFocus: Designing interaction techniques that support effective videoconferencing while participants are moving, addressing limited screen space, divided attention, mobility constraints, and temporary interruptions. The project explores microgestures, augmented spatial workspaces, and micro-asynchrony.
collaboration: Remote participants collaborate synchronously through videoconferencing while using different devices and operating in different physical environments. Mobile participants must coordinate with others despite interruptions, shifting attention, and limited interaction capabilities. The project investigates techniques for maintaining participation and shared awareness during these disruptions.
evaluation: Planned focus-group interviews, participatory design workshops, and controlled laboratory experiments investigating mobile videoconferencing practices and interaction techniques. The research examines engagement, comprehension, divided attention, and collaborative effectiveness. Specific team-level collaboration measures are not clearly defined.
myResearch: Moderately relevant to maintaining participation and conversational continuity under mobility, interruptions and divided attention. The project investigates videoconferencing on the move rather than co-navigation of physical AR and remote VR attendees.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Navigating Expertise Across Space and Time: Augmented Reality Points of Instruction for Remote Mentoring
researchFocus: Designing augmented reality interaction techniques that enable remote experts to create spatially anchored gestural instructions, called *Points of Instruction*, which trainees can independently access across space and time. The project investigates how to preserve and align instructions with physical environments that change during task execution.
collaboration: Remote experts and local trainees collaborate across heterogeneous virtual and physical environments, primarily in one-to-one or one-to-two mentoring scenarios. Experts create spatial instructions in virtual or 3D environments, while trainees access and execute them through AR. The project supports both synchronous guidance and asynchronous access to expert instructions.
evaluation: Planned field studies, participatory design workshops, and controlled experiments with surgical trainees. Evaluations examine spatial alignment accuracy, instruction fidelity, task performance, error rates, completion time, and learning retention using established surgical assessment measures such as OSATS.
myResearch: Low relevance through spatially anchored communication across physical and virtual settings. Its primary aim is remote instruction, including asynchronous mentoring, rather than spontaneous group interaction.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Investigating the Use of Co-Embodiment and Kinesthetic Co-Manipulation for Improving Technical Skill Learning in Virtual Reality
researchFocus: Investigating how virtual co-embodiment and kinesthetic co-manipulation improve technical skill learning and long-term retention in VR. The project examines shared control, sense of agency, joint agency, and multimodal guidance.
collaboration: An expert and a trainee collaborate through shared avatar control and kinesthetic interaction in a virtual environment. The project explores how different levels of control and physical guidance influence joint action, skill transfer, and learning.
evaluation: Two planned experimental studies comparing co-embodiment, kinesthetic guidance, and their combination, including dynamically adjusted control levels. Measures include sense of agency, EEG, temporal binding, task accuracy, completion time, and long-term skill retention.
myResearch: Only indirectly related. Shared avatar control and kinesthetic feedback offer a broader perspective on joint agency, but the study focuses on dyadic technical-skill learning rather than hybrid social-group transitions.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified

title: Maintaining Physical Collaboration in Virtual Reality
researchFocus: Designing intelligent interaction techniques that maintain physical collaboration between remote VR users with heterogeneous physical environments and haptic interfaces. The project explores AI-based adaptation of haptic feedback and visual representations to support consistent collaborative interaction.
collaboration: Remote participants collaborate synchronously in a shared VR environment while using different physical spaces and haptic devices. The project investigates how adaptive haptic feedback can support joint object manipulation and coordinated physical interaction despite differences in hardware capabilities.
evaluation: The research identifies evaluation challenges involving heterogeneous haptic setups, system latency, visual–haptic consistency, and collaborative task performance. Specific planned experimental protocols and collaboration-quality measures remain to be verified.
myResearch: Low relevance through variation in collaborators’ physical environments. The postdoc focuses on AI-adapted haptic co-manipulation between VR users, not the spatial and conversational coordination of AR–VR event participants.
evidenceStatus: Proposal-level description; outcomes not yet verified
